L2 and L3 are regular, so their concatenation L2.L3 is regular (regular languages are closed under concatenation). A context-free language intersected with a regular language is always context-free (a standard closure property), so the result is context-free.
Regular languages are a subset of context-free languages, and CFLs are closed under union, so a CFL unioned with a regular language is always a context-free language.

Union of two equivalence relations stays reflexive and symmetric; taking the transitive closure only adds pairs needed for transitivity and preserves reflexivity and symmetry, so the result is again an equivalence relation.

A pushdown automaton becomes as powerful as a Turing machine once it has two stacks (two auxiliary stacks can simulate a Turing machine's tape).
A tree is acyclic by definition, so it contains zero circuits regardless of the number of nodes.
A tree can be characterized as a minimally connected graph — connected, but removing any single edge disconnects it.
Every connected graph has at least one spanning tree; the minimum possible number of spanning trees a connected graph can have is 1 (achieved when the graph is itself already a tree).
The rank of a graph is defined as n - k, the number of vertices minus the number of connected components.
The nullity (circuit rank) of a graph is defined as e - n + k, edges minus vertices plus components.
A tree has a unique path between any two vertices — that uniqueness (no cycles) is exactly what makes it a tree.
To disconnect a vertex from a complete graph Kn you must remove all n-1 edges incident to it, and that is the minimum cut, so the edge connectivity is n-1.
A circuit passing through every vertex exactly once is a Hamiltonian circuit, by definition.
A Hamiltonian path visits all n vertices exactly once, using n-1 edges to connect them in sequence.
A connected graph is Eulerian iff every vertex has even degree — this guarantees an Eulerian circuit exists.
For a connected graph with n vertices, the incidence matrix has rank n-1 (one row is always a linear combination of the others).
If k is stated to be the number of colors actually required for a proper coloring, that k is, by definition, the chromatic number.
With no edges at all, no two vertices are adjacent, so a single color suffices — the graph is 1-chromatic regardless of n.
Having at least one edge means its two endpoints must get different colors, so at least 2 colors are required.
In a complete graph Kn every pair of vertices is adjacent, so all n vertices need distinct colors — it is n-chromatic.
The Four Color Theorem states that every planar graph can be properly colored with at most 4 colors.
By the subset construction, every NFA can be converted into an equivalent DFA, so a DFA can always simulate an NFA.
(a|b)(a|b) concatenates two independent choices of a or b, producing every 2-letter string over {a,b}: aa, ab, ba, bb.
'(a|b)*' allows any number (including zero) of a's and b's in any combination, matching 'zero or more instances of a and b'.

'(a|b)*' generates every possible string (including the empty string) over the alphabet {a,b}.
A simple FSM reads its input once, left to right, with no ability to move back or reread — equivalent to a Turing machine with a finite tape, no rewind, and unidirectional movement.
A Turing machine's infinite read-write tape lets it remember arbitrarily long input sequences and revisit them, which is exactly the extra power an FSM (bounded to its finite states) lacks.
Context-sensitive languages are exactly the languages recognized by linear bounded automata (a Turing machine restricted to tape length proportional to the input).
Context-free languages are closed under union, concatenation ('product'), and Kleene star, but not under complementation (or intersection) in general.
Recognizing even palindromes requires guessing the midpoint of the string, which needs nondeterminism; a deterministic PDA cannot do this, but a nondeterministic PDA can.

The standard finite automaton 5-tuple is (Q, Σ, δ, q0, F) — states, input alphabet, transition function, start state, and accepting states. An output alphabet belongs to Mealy/Moore machines (6-tuples), not a plain acceptor automaton.

A context-free language is inherently ambiguous exactly when every context-free grammar generating it is ambiguous — no unambiguous CFG exists for it.

In most standard textbook treatments, both Moore and Mealy machines are defined as 6-tuples (states, input alphabet, output alphabet, transition function, output function, start state) — they differ in how the output function is defined, not in tuple size.

A mapping is surjective (onto) when every element of the codomain has at least one pre-image in the domain.
A partially ordered set (poset) is a set equipped with a binary relation that is reflexive, antisymmetric, and transitive.
A lattice is a poset in which every pair of elements has both a least upper bound (join) and a greatest lower bound (meet).
